title: Double Dose of Speedrun! | Queens Gambit Accepted | The Sensei Speedrun | GM Naroditsky

moves.spoken: Meeting the c-pawn with e6 heads for a Queen's Gambit Declined structure — and there's a hidden bonus: as a QGD player you barely need to study the English at all, which slashes the amount of theory you have to carry.

Capturing on d5 this early is simply a bad move — it releases the central tension prematurely, hands over better control of the middle, and is completely toothless. It's a sign the opening's ideas aren't fully understood.
There's no single right way to develop, but a fine plan is the bishop to d6 followed, London-style, by c6 — a compact, harmonious shell that's easy to handle in any move order.

Now the question of the light-squared bishop. It wants the good diagonal, but a pawn move to prepare it would weaken the kingside — so instead insert a flexible move first, a rook to e8. It's a square the rook is simply happy on, and it quietly rules out an annoying central knight leap. When unsure, play the move you know can't hurt.

Here's the elegant way to get the bishop to its diagonal without the weakening pawn push: develop to g4, then swing it around via h5 toward g6 — no hurry, it's happy where it sits. And a strategic point on the queenside: most players would automatically stop the pawn expansion, but you can allow it and then freeze the pawn in place, which isn't good for the opponent at all. Then a rook-pawn nudge puts the question to the pinning bishop. If it retreats to a square where a pawn is its lone defender, watch for an overload — one pawn guarding two things at once is a defender stretched too thin. And the meta-lesson of the finish: the hallmark of the great attackers is knowing when to just play simple. Don't chase the brilliancy prize and leave points on the table — a clean pawn grab ends it, and even then order of operations matters: the right capture sequence leaves the opponent unable to recapture in any legal way.

Be aware of the transposition — a central pawn push here would steer into a Catalan, which is a demanding, theory-heavy opening best left alone below master strength, since it asks you to be comfortable a pawn down for long stretches.
With the tension released, the bishop develops freely and the second player is, if anything, already slightly the better side — the premature capture yielded the centre for nothing.

And a crucial structural warning: don't develop the knight to c6 in these positions. Beginners do it for lack of understanding that the d5 pawn must be kept under lock and key — the knight blocks the c-pawn, so a knight-and-bishop set-up starts pressing d5 while it can't be properly defended. The very same trap catches players in the Caro-Kann for exactly the same reason.
